caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 593 of 1991
lawyer:
Mohammad Ali, Advocate ----- For the Appellants. 
Abdul Awal, Advocate ----- For the Respondent.
parties:
Sonali Bank and another ------ Appellants
VS
Md Harun ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
2. The short fact leading to this appeal is that the plaintiff instituted the suit alleging that for obtaining loan under IDA credit he applied before the local Sonali Bank Feni for establishment of Rana Oil Mill. The defendant for the establishment and running of the Rice Mill agreed to give certain benefits to the plaintiff and on getting the assurance of assistance the plaintiff took a plan for establishment of the aforesaid Oil Mill. On consultation with the bank the plaintiff applied for loan under IDA credit. The project was for Taka 51,46,120.00 which was approved by the bank and they sanctioned a sum of Taka 9.70 lac from IDA credit of which Taka 7.00 lac was for capital investment and Taka 2.70 lac as working capital. 

 3. It is the case of the plaintiff that under IDA project plaintiff was to receive 70% of the project money and 30% will be from the investor's own fund. But in spite of this the plaintiff was favoured with 35% loan from IDA credit. His further case is that, in addition to that the plaintiff was to spend Taka 20.00 lac for the project from his own fund, As the bank has not given him 70% from the IDA credit the plaintiff had to spend Taka 10,37,120.00 from his own pocket. His further case is that, when the defendant bank failed to pay 70% of the IDA credit the plaintiff applied for the balance 35% from IDA credit. But the defendant bank instead of making payment under IDA credit saddled him with a cash credit amount of Taka 3.00 lac from their own fund. When the plaintiff failed to run the mill due to non payment of the aforesaid amount he applied for further amount and after negotiation the bank increased the cash credit limit to Taka 4.00 lac but at the same time they deducted the IDA credit amount already received by the plaintiff resulting in the plaintiff's failure to run the mill properly. When the plaintiff prayed for further amount the defendant bank wanted hypothecation of the goods which the plaintiff refused. The bank also demanded further security though the entire project was under the security and mortgage with the bank the value of which is over Taka 50.00 lac.. It is the case of the plaintiff that the bank most illegally realised IDA credit amount from the cash credit amount though these are under two separate agreements. The bank had no authority to realise this IDA credit amount from cash credit amount before the IDA credit amount has been matured. It is the case of the plaintiff that before the instalment under IDA became due the bank realised this by deducting the same from cash credit amount. Their further case is that this resulted in the stoppage of the mill and causing a huge loss to the plaintiff. The plaintiff also asserted that the bank also thrust upon the plaintiff a transformer valued at Taka 1.50 lac and the value of that was also deducted from cash credit amount. Their case is that before the loan became due the defendant issued notice asking for repayment of the same. The plaintiff also asserted that in 1988 there was an audit of the bank and it was reported that due to the activities of the bank management the Oil mill had to be stopped causing a huge loss and the bank officials have been made responsible for this stoppage. It is the case of the plaintiff that due to these activities of the bank officials the mill had to be stopped causing mental sufferings and torture to the plaintiff who invested the entire savings of his life in the mill with the hope that he will be provided with 70% of the project money from IDA credit for establishing this industry and this closure of the industry has caused ill reputation of the plaintiff and also destroyed the project. The plaintiff suffered huge loss due to the retrenchment of the staff and the whole project has been destroyed causing huge loss to the plaintiff. The plaintiff demanded Taka 10.00  lac for the loss of his reputation and prestige, another sum of Taka 10.00 lac for damage to his portion, another Taka 10.00 lac for menial torture, another Taka 5.00 lac for damage of the project and another Taka 6 lac for stoppage of the mill up to 1993. In all the plaintiff demanded Taka 1,36,46,120 from the bank. Subsequently, the plaint was amended and the demand was made for Taka 60.00 lac as loss during four years of stoppage of the mill. 

 4. Before the trial Court defendants 1 and 2 entered appearance and contested the suit by filing joint written statement. In that written statement they alleged that the mill was established as joint venture project of the plaintiff and the defendants and it was not established by the plaintiff himself. Their case is that, on 5-10-83 the plaintiff applied for loan from IDA credit scheme which was examined and the project value was fixed at Taka 25,57,120.00. Their case is that in all Taka 24,57,120.00 (Taka twenty four lac fifty seven thousand one hundred twenty) only was spent for establishing the project. The bank granted an amount of Taka 9.70 lac for 3rd IDA credit scheme and it was stipulated that the loan is to be repaid in 12 installments and payment will be made in June and December of each year. It was also stipulated that in addition to the advance made by the bank the plaintiff will bear the other expenses and if the plaintiff fails to repay the installments in due time he will be bound to repay the entire amount to the bank and the plaintiff accepted the proposal of the bank by putting signatures in the documents and it was stipulated that the 1st installment was to be paid in June 1985. Their further case is that on 28-5-84 the plaintiff applied for cash credit advance for a sum of Taka 5.00 lac and the bank on 1-9-84 allowed a sum of Taka  3.00 lac as such credit advance which the plaintiff  accepted, This amount was subsequently raised to Taka 4.00 lac. Their further case is that the plaintiff is to pay the bank a sum of Taka  22,57,120.00 on 27-5-90 and though the plaintiff  received Taka 4.00 as case) credit there was no raw  material in the mill and he spent the money elsewhere. He also failed to pay the installment subsequently and when he failed to pay the same the bank instituted Money suit No. 1 of 1990 on 3-6-90. Their further case is that, the bank is not at all responsible for any loss alleged to have been sustained by the plaintiff in running the industry and for avoiding the repayment of the bank's loan the present suit has been filed. 

 7. Mr Mohammad Ali, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant, submits that the plaintiff received a sum of Taka 9.70 lac from the bank under IDA credit scheme and he also received another sum of Taka 3.00 lac as cash credit which was subsequently raised to Taka 4.00 lac. But instead of using these amounts in the project the plaintiff diverted this amount to other business resulting in the stoppage of the Oil Mill, He failed to repay the 1st installment or any installment of the loan taken from the bank and the mill was stopped due to non utilization of the amount taken from the bank for no fault of the appellant. The plaintiff respondent diverted the money to other purposes for which he failed to run the mill. The learned Advocate contends that there was a scheme for repayment of the loan. But the plaintiff failed to follow this scheme and also failed to repay the bank's money for which a notice was issued and subsequently a suit was filed which was decreed. 

 8. It was contended that without any fault of the bank the Mill stopped its operation. The learned Counsel submits that the trial Court assessed an amount of Taka 2.00 lac as compensation for loss of reputation of the plaintiff without any evidence and so is the case with assessment of another sum of Taka 2.00 lac for damage and loss to the project. The learned Advocate contends that as regards the assessment of Taka 6.86 lac as a loss for stoppage of the Mill there is absolutely no evidence or date and the plaintiff also failed to prove that he suffered a loss of Taka 1,43,100.00 for retrenchment of mill staffs due to stoppage of the Mill. The learned Advocate contends that the assessment made by the trial Court has no basis. This is simply arbitrary. It is argued that in such a suit where compensation and damages have been claimed the plaintiff has to prove the loss by adducing convincing evidence. But no such evidence has been adduced. The trial Court, according to Mr Mohammad Ali, failed to appreciate the evidence on record properly and came to, the wrong finding which requires interference. 

 9. Mr Abdul Awal, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff respondent, on the other hand, submits that in this matter it is an admitted fact that when the plaintiff applied for loan under 3rd IDA credit scheme the project was inquired into and evaluated by the bank officials and they assessed the value at Taka 24,57,120.00. It is the case of the plaintiff that the bank advanced Taka 9.70 lac on two heads for the project which is 35% of the project value and not 70% as required under the IDA credit scheme. The plaintiff applied for further sum from IDA credit for running the mill. But instead of making any payment from that account the bank saddled the plaintiff with cash credit scheme for an amount of Taka 3.00 lac initially which was subsequently raised to Taka 4.00 lac. It is also submitted that the plaintiff repaid some money out of the advance but the bank deducted the loan amount from the cash credit account resulting in the shortage of fund of the plaintiff in running the industry and that the plaintiff applied for capital for running the industry and that the cash credit scheme was imposed is an admitted fact. It is also submitted that the plaintiff entered into an agreement with the bank for getting Taka 9.70 lac under IDA credit scheme and for the cash credit advance the plaintiff had to enter into a fresh agreement with the defendant bank. The learned Advocate contends that the bank deducted the alleged overdue loan amount from cash credit advance, meaning thereby that nothing in cash has been paid to the plaintiff for running the industry. For all these the plaintiff instituted this suit and claimed compensation. 

 10. It appears from the record that it was not stipulated either in the sanction letter of the IDA project loan or in the cash credit advance that the bank reserves the right to deduct the IDA credit amount from the cash credit advance. The bank in this case it appears failed to appreciate that these two loans are distinct and different. They at the time of giving advance under cash credit deducted the IDA amount thereby giving no benefit to the plaintiff for which he applied for further loan which was sanctioned in the form of cash credit. The plaintiff it appears applied to the bank for giving him more money from IDA scheme so that he can run the industry as he was in shortage of fund. But it appears that instead of making any further payment under IDA scheme the bank proposed cash credit advance which the plaintiff had to accept under painful circumstances and he also failed to get anything when the IDA was adjusted. This resulted in stoppage of the mill and the plaintiff was left without any amount with him so that he may run the mill. Admittedly, the mill was in operation for almost about two years and then it stopped due to lack of finance. It is also an admitted fact that the plaintiff had to spend more money out of his own pocket for land development, construction of the mill house, installation of electricity and all these amounting to Taka 10.00 lac and it is the case of the plaintiff that while approving the project this amount was not considered by the appellant bank. Before the trial Court the plaintiff got himself examined as PW 1 and he deposed that as per the IDA credit rules he was to pay back the amount within 12 years though in the agreement it was stipulated to be paid back within 7 years and working capital within 4 years. He deposed that he had to sign this agreement being compelled as he has already invested his lifelong savings in the project. He deposed that on seeing the scheme that 70% will be advanced under 3rd IDA credit he applied for the loan and invested the money hoping that he will get this amount but he was not favoured with that. He further deposed that in the sanction letter it was stipulated that the mill was to run in one shift and it would be profitable if it is run in three shifts. This witness deposed that when he applied for further loan under IDA scheme he was saddled with cash credit amount of Taka 3.00 lac on 1-9-84 which of course was subsequently. raised to Taka 4.00 lac. But at the same time they deducted the IDA amount from this cash credit limit. The activities of the bank officials resulted in the stoppage of the industry causing loss and damage for which he had to institute the present suit. 

 11. It appears that before the trial Court one Abul Kashem, a Senior Officer of the defendant bank, was examined as DW 1. and he also stated that the plaintiff respondent applied for IDA credit which was subsequently sanctioned and on the basis of the feasibility and expert reports a sum of Taka 9.70 lac was paid to the plaintiff. He further submits that in addition to this amount the bank also paid Taka 4.00 lac to the plaintiff respondent. It is in his evidence that they paid Taka 6.76 lac as working capital of the plaintiff by cheques. But with that amount the plaintiff has not purchased the goods. His simple evidence in examination-in-chief is that the plaintiff is not entitled to any compensation as prayed for. During cross examination he admitted that in the IDA scheme it was stipulated that the recovery period is to be 12 years with a grace period of 2/3 years. But in spite of that they fixed the recovery period at 7 years and 4.5 years. He further admitted that though the plaintiff demanded Taka 25,54,760 but they sanctioned Taka 24,57,120 as project loan and on different occasions Taka 9.70 lac was paid which is roughly equivalent to 35% of the sanctioned project amount. During cross examination this witness plainly admitted that in accepting the proposal to set up the industry and fixing the project value of Taka 24,57,120 the bank has not considered the amount the plaintiff invested in land development, electrification, layout, documentation and expenses for show room, etc. including the construction of the factory building. He further admitted that the local Manager requested the AGM vide letters dated 22-11-88 and 26-10-89 for giving more loans to the plaintiff. 

 12. These are the oral evidence adduced before the trial Court. It appears from the perusal of the record that the cash credit account was fully adjusted. What remains to be realised from the plaintiff was the advance made from 3rd IDA credit scheme. It further appears that time and again the plaintiff wanted further loan for running the industry which the bank was bound to pay in view of the terms of the IDA credit and the sanction letter. Now from the materials on record it appears that though the bank extended the cash credit limit to Taka 4.00 lac but they actually paid Taka 25,000.00 from that account. We have already found that these are two distinct and separate accounts and contracts arid for one the other one cannot be disturbed. So by giving or sanctioning cash credit on the one hand the IDA credit ought not to have been taken back that is, giving by one hand and taking away by another hand which is not legal and against the canons of natural justice. This cash credit was required by the plaintiff for running the mill. He never applied for the cash credit loan from the bank but he applied for giving further advance under IDA credit. But the bank at their wisdom instead of giving IDA credit offered this amount from credit scheme and got the agreement signed by the plaintiff. When the bank adjusted the IDA credit amount from the cash credit the plaintiff was left with no money to run the mill and he had to close down the industry for lack of running capital and it appears from the evidence that the cash credit limit was raised to Taka 4.00 lac six months after the closure of the mill. It further appears that when the bank raised the amount of Taka 4.00 lac they initially wanted to deduct Taka 1.40 lac from that account which was made a condition precedent and the plaintiff had to accept that under painful circumstances. But even then the IDA amount was deducted from the cash credit amount leaving nothing for the plaintiff for running the mill. Admittedly the plaintiff received the loan amount and set up the mill and put the same in operation in August 1984 and out of the sanctioned amount of Taka 24,57,920 the bank admittedly paid only 35% of that amount though the IDA scheme required that the plaintiff be paid 70% of the project amount. It further appears that the cash credit account was fully adjusted on 13-9-86 and the mill was closed down in September 1986. From the materials on record it appears that there was clear deviation and violation of IDA credit circular as well as the terms of the contract. The defendant bank was required to provide the plaintiff with sufficient fund as running capital for running the oil mill. But for reasons best known to them created obstructions in running the mill which was in operation for about two years and then it was closed down for lack of running capital. 

 13. It is the definite case of the plaintiff respondent that when the bank failed to abide by the agreement in supplying adequate fund for running the industry and when admittedly the industry was established under the loan taken from IDA credit scheme .and when the bank failed to provide the running capital as may be required under the agreement the plaintiff had to close down the mill. It is the definite case of the plaintiff that this has resulted in the loss to the plaintiff for which he had to institute the present suit. From the perusal of the evidence on record and considering the facts and circumstances of the case the trial Court found that the mill had to be closed down due to non co-operation of the appellant bank and on consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case we also hold the same view. It appears from the perusal of the record that the plaintiff demanded compensation to the tune of Taka 10 lac for loss of his prestige in the locality and another sum of Taka 10.00 lac for sustaining mental torture and a sum of Taka 5.00 lac was demanded as compensation for damage to the project and Taka 60.00 lac was demanded as compensation for the closure of the mill and also the plaintiff demanded compensation for the retrenchment of staff. The trial Court, it appears on consideration of the evidence on record, awarded a sum of Taka 2.00 lac towards the loss of reputation and for mental torture and for damage of the enterprise compensation was assessed at Taka 2.00 lac and compensation for .stoppage of the mill was assessed at Taka 6.86 lac and also a sum of Taka 1,43,100.00 f6r retrenchment of the staff. 

 14. Admittedly, excepting PW 1 no other witness was examined to prove that the plaintiff’s reputation suffered due to stoppage of the mill or failure to run the mill. In such a case the onus lies heavily on the plaintiff to prove that his reputation suffered or questioned due to the failure of the project or closure of the mill No. one came to depose that when the mill was closed they formed an adverse opinion. There is absolutely no evidence on that count and in that view of the matter when there is no corroborative evidence we hold that the trial Court has wrongly assessed Taka 1.00 lac on that count which the plaintiff is not entitled: As regards the second item which is mental torture and damage to the entrepreneurship for which Taka 2.00 lac was assessed by the trial Court admittedly before going to start the mill the plaintiff had long negotiation with the bank and under their guidance he invested his own money in land development, building construction, electrification etc. and then he applied for the loan under 3rd IDA scheme and there was evaluation of the project and the valuation of the project was assessed at Taka 24.57 lac and odd but the bank paid only Taka 9.70 lac in all to the plaintiff and the mill started its operation and thereafter due to non co-operation of the bank in providing credit facilities. for which they were bound under the contract the plaintiff had to close down the industry. Admittedly the plaintiff himself invested a huge amount and then at the instance of the bank established the industry which had to be closed down due to non co-operation of the bank and for that matter we hold that the plaintiff had to suffer mental loss and agony and for that the trial Court rightly and correctly assessed a sum of Taka 2.00 lac as compensation. 

 15. The trial Court it appears has assessed compensation of Taka 6.86 lac as loss due to the closure of the mill for four years. This amount the trial Court assessed on the basis of the project value of the mill that was over Taka 24.00 lac and there the bank paid 9.70 lac. The trial Court found that a transformer was thrashed upon the shoulder of the plaintiff which was valued at Taka 1.50 lac and it deducted this amount making the advance at Taka 8.20 lac He also deducted this amount from the total costs of the project amounting to Taka 24.00 lac and found that there remains only Taka 22.50 lac for project out of which if Taka 8.20 lac is deducted then there remains Taka 14.30 lac which is involved in the project and taking the round figure of Taka 14.00 lac the trial Court assessed the compensation at the rate of 13% per annum .amounting to Taka 1.72 lac per year and as the mill was closed for four years it came to Taka 6.86 lac. We have considered this aspect of the matter but we failed to agree with the finding on deduction of Taka 1.50 lac on the head of the price of the transformer as the transformer was issued in the project. So for assessment of the compensation this amount cannot be deducted. The plaintiff got Taka 9.70 lac from the bank and the project was for Taka 24.09 lac and if this amount is deducted then total comes down to Taka 14.30 lac. The trial Court it appears failed to appreciate another aspect of the matter and it is the investment made by the plaintiff from his own fund before getting any money from the bank for land development, building construction, electrification, documentation, etc. and, according to the plaintiff, he spent Taka 10.00 lac. It appears that this plaintiff had invested his good money for the said purpose has been admitted by DW 1. But as regards the actual figure of the amount spent there is no evidence. The plaintiff has not produced any paper to prove that actually he spent Taka 10.00 lac. The expenditure is admitted but not the figure. In such a situation when the project value was assessed at over Taka 24.00 lac and when such a mill has been established we hold that we can safely assess the land development and construction cost at Taka 5.00 lac and when the plaintiff spent this amount from his own pocket and when due to the aforesaid grounds the mill had to be closed down we hold that the plaintiff is also entitled to compensation over that amount as well. So, the total figure comes down to Taka 14.30 lac + 5.00 lac that means Taka 19.30 lac and the trial Court assessed the compensation at the rate of 13% interest per annum over Taka 14.00 lac. The rate of interest or profit or loss that has been assessed by the trial Court is the proper rate and we do not like to interfere in the matter. The calculation of loss will now be over Taka 19.30 lac and on calculation we came to the finding that the annual amount of compensation will be Taka 2.50 lac which comes down to Taka 10.36 lac in four years’ time. 

 16. It is the case of the plaintiff before the trial Court that after starting of mill he had to employ several persons for running the mill and when the mill was closed down the plaintiff had to retrench those staffs for which he had to pay Taka 1.43 lac to those staffs and in support of this the plaintiff produced Exhibit 15 from which it appears that he employed a good number of staffs for running the mill and admittedly they were retrenched when the mill was closed down. In such a situation the plaintiff had to pay Taka 1.43 lac to those people which has been supported by Exhibit 15 and the trial Court assessed this amount as compensation and we are in full agreement with the trial Court. 

 17. It may be argued in this case that when the plaintiff has not appealed against the judgment and decree or the assessment he cannot be given any further relief in this appeal when we intend to assess the compensation for the invested amount by the plaintiff himself for land development, building construction electrification, etc. But Order 41 rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure has given us this power to assess compensation which escaped the notice of the trial Court and acting under this provision of the Code and for doing complete justice when the mill had been closed down due to non co-operation of the bank we are inclined to assess the compensation on the aforesaid head and we take the help in this matter from the decision reported in 37 DLR (AD) 63 (Md Osman Gani vs Mst Kulsum Bibi and ors). The respondent could have filed a cross-objection but mere non-filing of the cross objection cannot be ground for not giving him a relief to which he is legally entitled.
